case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: G.S. v. Department of Human Services
key_cases.holding: The Court held that the 'minimum degree of care' in N.J.S.A. 9:6-8.21(c)(4) means grossly or wantonly negligent conduct, not ordinary negligence, and affirmed the neglect finding against a caregiver who recklessly over-medicated a child.
key_cases.relevance: G.S. supplies the culpability standard every substantiated neglect finding in New Jersey must satisfy.
key_cases.quote: the phrase "minimum degree of care" refers to conduct that is grossly or wantonly negligent, but not necessarily intentional

key_cases.case_name: Department of Children & Families, Division of Youth & Family Services v. T.B.
key_cases.holding: The Court reversed a substantiated neglect finding and ordered the mother's name removed from the Child Abuse Registry because leaving a child briefly without confirming a grandparent was home was negligent but not grossly negligent.
key_cases.relevance: T.B. holds that a substantiation must rest on gross negligence or recklessness, not on an ordinary parenting lapse.
key_cases.quote: every failure to perform a cautionary act is not abuse or neglect.

key_cases.case_name: Department of Children & Families v. E.D.-O.
key_cases.holding: The Court held that imminent risk is measured at the time of the triggering event but that a categorical approach is improper, and remanded the mother's substantiation to the Office of Administrative Law for a hearing on the totality of the circumstances.
key_cases.relevance: E.D.-O. entitles a parent contesting a substantiated finding to an individualized OAL hearing rather than categorical treatment.
key_cases.quote: We also hold that the Division should have referred the mother's appeal to the OAL for a hearing.

key_cases.case_name: S.C. v. New Jersey Department of Children and Families
key_cases.holding: The Court upheld the Department's 'not established' investigative category but required improved notice, a credible-evidence basis, and an informal opportunity to respond, while rejecting any right to a contested OAL hearing.
key_cases.relevance: S.C. contrasts the formal hearing rights that attach to substantiated findings with the informal process for 'not established' findings.
key_cases.quote: We reject that due process considerations require the Department to conduct an adjudicative contested case proceeding either internally or at the Office of Administrative Law for a "not established" finding.

key_cases.case_name: In re Allegations of Physical Abuse at Blackacre Academy
key_cases.court: New Jersey Superior Court, Appellate Division
key_cases.holding: The court upheld the Institutional Abuse Investigation Unit's substantiated finding, holding the unit could report its results to the Department of Education and the affected parents and was not required to hold a hearing first.
key_cases.relevance: Blackacre addresses the process due before a substantiated institutional finding is entered in the Central Registry.
key_cases.quote: the IAIU was not required to conduct a formal or informal hearing before placing appellants' names in the Central Registry

key_cases.case_name: N.J. Department of Children & Families v. R.R.
key_cases.court: New Jersey Superior Court, Appellate Division
key_cases.holding: The court reversed a 'not established' finding as unsupported by the record and directed that the allegation be deemed 'unfounded' so the records would be treated accordingly.
key_cases.relevance: R.R. applies arbitrary-and-capricious review to the Division's investigative findings.
key_cases.quote: As we find that the Division erred in finding the allegation was "not established," the Division shall deem the allegation to be "unfounded" and treat the records accordingly.

key_cases.case_name: New Jersey Division of Youth & Family Services v. P.W.R.
key_cases.holding: The Court reversed the abuse-or-neglect finding, holding the record inadequate to establish a Title 9 violation and that an occasional slap to a teenager's face as discipline, causing no bruising or marks, is not 'excessive corporal punishment' under N.J.S.A. 9:6-8.21(c)(4)(b).
key_cases.relevance: P.W.R. supplies the substantive corporal-punishment standard that a substantiated physical-abuse finding in New Jersey must satisfy.
key_cases.quote: Limiting state involvement only to interference with excessive corporal punishment requires the exercise of judgment by reviewing courts before a finding of physical abuse is entered against a parent.

key_cases.case_name: New Jersey Division of Youth & Family Services v. V.T.
key_cases.court: New Jersey Superior Court, Appellate Division
key_cases.holding: The court reversed a neglect finding based on a father's positive cocaine and marijuana tests at two supervised visits, holding that drug use without expert proof of impairment or of actual or imminent harm to the child does not establish neglect.
key_cases.relevance: V.T. is the Appellate Division companion to A.L. and Y.N., holding a substantiation cannot rest on drug use alone absent proof of risk to the particular child.
key_cases.quote: Contrary to the trial judge's conclusion, use of illegal drugs days prior to a supervised visit does not as a matter of law constitute neglect.

key_cases.case_name: New Jersey Division of Child Protection and Permanency v. J.R.-R.
key_cases.holding: The Court reversed and remanded for a new hearing, holding that Title 9 nowhere authorizes shifting the burden of proof to parents to disprove culpability and that the family court's use of conditional res ipsa loquitur denied the parents a fundamentally fair hearing.
key_cases.relevance: J.R.-R. is the most recent Supreme Court statement of the proofs required for a substantiated finding, barring the Division from substantiating against multiple caregivers by burden-shifting when it cannot prove who caused the harm.
key_cases.quote: The family court's mistaken conception that the burden of proof shifted to Jenny and George rendered its factfindings fatally flawed and denied the parents a fundamentally fair hearing.

state_agency.name: New Jersey Division of Child Protection and Permanency

timeline_requirements.deadline: Immediately upon receipt of the report; investigation initiated within 24 hours
timeline_requirements.starts_from: The Division's receipt of a report of child abuse or neglect
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Not specified in N.J.S.A. 9:6-8.11; a delay in initiating the investigation is permitted only where the Division or other designated entity authorizes it at the request of a law enforcement official.

timeline_requirements.starts_from: State Central Registry assigns the CPS report to the local office for response
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Good cause must be established and an extension approved by the local office manager or designee before day 60 (CP&P-II-C-6-200).
